passage: In Seville, ten-year-old Mateo ran home waving his maths test. "A ten! Hana, look!" His big sister clapped, and he glowed all evening. On Thursday the spelling test came back with a six. Mateo stuffed it in his bag and wouldn't come to dinner. "I'm just stupid," he said into his pillow. "I'm not good at anything." Hana sat on the edge of his bed. "On Monday you were a genius and today you're stupid? You're the same Mateo." He didn't look up. "It doesn't feel like that."

qa.q: What mark did Mateo get on the spelling test?
qa.a: He got a six.

qa.q: Why does Mateo feel "stupid" after one spelling test?
qa.a: He seems to feel worthwhile only when he scores high, so one poor mark feels like proof he isn't good enough.

qa.q: What could Hana or his parents try in the weeks ahead?
qa.a: They could notice his effort and kindness, not just his marks, so his sense of worth stops rising and falling with each test.

qa.q: What is it like for Hana to see Mateo glow on Monday and crumble on Thursday?
qa.a: It is probably confusing and sad for her, because she sees him as the same brother either way.

grounding: A ten-year-old feels valuable after a high mark and crumbles after a low one, treating an ordinary setback as proof he is not enough.

passage: At the Jaipur school's quiz finals, Yogesh, eleven, stood frozen on the stage when the host announced that his team had come second. Everyone clapped. Yogesh didn't. Backstage he kicked a chair and hissed, "Second is losing. Papa only puts first prizes on the fridge." Urmila ma'am, the quiz coach, found him behind the curtain, cheeks wet. "You answered the hardest question of the day," she said. "I watched you work it out." He shook his head. "Doesn't count. We didn't win." Urmila ma'am sat on the step beside him and said nothing more for a while.

qa.q: Which place did Yogesh's team get?
qa.a: They came second.

qa.q: What does Yogesh's "Second is losing" suggest about how he sees himself?
qa.a: It suggests he feels good enough only when he wins, so even second place leaves him upset and feeling like a failure.

qa.q: What might help Yogesh after a day like this?
qa.a: Adults could keep pointing out his effort and thinking, as Urmila ma'am did, and his family could celebrate more than first prizes.

qa.q: How might Yogesh's teammates feel if he calls second place losing?
qa.a: They might feel their good result is being dismissed, and some may feel less proud.

grounding: An eleven-year-old whose worth depends on winning treats second place as failure, even when a coach praises his thinking.

passage: The science test came back with 14 out of 20 in red, and Rekha folded it into a tiny square before anyone could see. All the way home in the school van she stared out of the window. At dinner she said she wasn't hungry. "Everyone got more than me. I'm the stupid one now," she told her elder brother, Sumit, when he found her crying on the balcony. "Last week you were the genius," he said. "Last week I got 19." Sumit sat down beside her. "So you're only good when the number's big?" Rekha didn't answer. She pressed the paper square tighter in her fist.

qa.q: What mark did Rekha get in the science test?
qa.a: 14 out of 20.

qa.q: How did Rekha feel about herself after the test?
qa.a: She felt ashamed and worthless, as if one lower mark proved she was stupid.

qa.q: How could Sumit or her parents help Rekha next?
qa.a: Show her she is valued whatever the mark, and talk about what she learned rather than the number.

qa.q: What might Sumit be thinking when he asks if she's only good when the number's big?
qa.a: He seems concerned that Rekha's sense of worth depends entirely on marks.

grounding: Shows a child whose sense of worth rises and falls with marks, crumbling after an ordinary poor result.

passage:
"Mumma, I came second."
"Second in the whole district drawing contest, Sumit! That's wonderful."
"It's not. Rishabh came first. So mine was worse."
Neelam put down the ladle. "Yours was a tiger in the rain. I loved the stripes."
"Nobody cares about second. You only put first-prize ones on the fridge."
"Did I say that?"
"You put Didi's gold certificate there."
Neelam was quiet. "Hmm. I did."
"If I'm not first, I'm nothing." Sumit kicked the chair leg. "I'm never entering again."

qa.q: What did Sumit draw?
qa.a: A tiger in the rain.

qa.q: Why did Sumit say "If I'm not first, I'm nothing"?
qa.a: He feels worthless and disappointed, believing only first place earns love and attention.

qa.q: What could Neelam do now to help?
qa.a: Praise the effort and ideas in the tiger drawing and display it too, so Sumit sees his worth isn't tied to winning.

qa.q: How might Neelam feel when Sumit mentions the fridge?
qa.a: Neelam seems surprised and uneasy, realising her own habit may have taught him that only winners count.

grounding: Illustrates a child who feels valued only when winning and crumbles after coming second.

passage: Last term I got 62 out of 100 in maths, and I didn't tell anyone for two days. I'm Ganga, and I'm the one who always gets the highest marks in our class. That's who I am. Or that's who I thought I was. When the paper came back, it felt like the ground had gone. I stopped talking in class. I didn't go for kho-kho. My friend Hansa asked what was wrong and I snapped at her. At home I tore out the page and hid it in my old pencil box. When Hansa said she'd got 58 and was fine, I couldn't understand how. For me, one bad mark felt like proof I wasn't good at all.

qa.q: Where did Ganga hide the page?
qa.a: In the old pencil box.

qa.q: What was Ganga feeling when the paper came back?
qa.a: Ganga felt crushed and ashamed, as if the ground had gone, because being top felt like Ganga's whole worth.

qa.q: What could help Ganga see a bad mark differently?
qa.a: Hearing from adults and friends that worth doesn't depend on marks, and treating the paper as a chance to learn.

qa.q: How might Hansa have felt when Ganga snapped?
qa.a: Hansa was probably hurt and puzzled, since she only asked what was wrong.

grounding: Shows a child whose worth depends on top marks, so one ordinary setback feels like proof of not being enough.

passage:
Class teacher's note, Class 5, maths results day.
Rashmi usually beams at full marks and runs to show me. Today she got 14 out of 25. She folded the paper small and pushed it deep into her bag. When Samir got the top mark, she whispered, "I'm the stupid one now." At lunch she didn't eat, and told a friend, "My mother will be so disappointed in me."
I sat beside her: "One test shows what we need to practise. It doesn't show who you are." She shook her head, eyes wet.
Next: tomorrow I've asked Rashmi to help me set up the science corner, a job that has nothing to do with marks. This week I will call her mother to share how kind and hardworking Rashmi is, and talk about praising effort at home.

qa.q: What mark did Rashmi get on the maths test?
qa.a: 14 out of 25.

qa.q: How did Rashmi feel after seeing her mark?
qa.a: She felt ashamed and not good enough, calling herself "the stupid one" and worrying that her mother would be disappointed.

qa.q: What steps did the teacher plan to help Rashmi feel valued beyond marks?
qa.a: Giving her the science corner job, which has nothing to do with marks, and calling her mother to talk about Rashmi's kindness and praising effort at home.

qa.q: How might Samir's top mark look from Rashmi's side?
qa.a: To Rashmi it may feel like proof that she has lost her place, since her sense of worth depends on being the one with high marks.

grounding: Shows a teacher noticing a child whose worth depends on marks crumbling after one poor result, and planning ways to show she is valued.
